newsitem.title: UK: Business group urges UK government to raise taxes.
newsitem.headline: Business group urges UK government to raise taxes.

text.p: More economic advice was issued to the next British government on Thursday when another big business lobby urged it to raise income tax, not interest rates, after the election to dampen consumer demand.

The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said the next Chancellor should increase income tax by one pence and not risk damaging the economy by fuelling the pound's rally with another interest rate rise.
The call came as its latest quarterly economic survey showed manufacturing and service sector firms saw their business hit by the strong pound in the first quarter.

"While many commentators believe that interest rates will have to rise after the election in order to contain inflation, this will have the damaging effect of hurting manufacturing investment and export competitiveness," said BCC president David Richardson.
"There is an alternative. In our view the new government must look at the option of tightening fiscal policy in order to subdue consumer demand without hurting competitiveness."
The call echoed advice delivered on Wednesday by the Confederation of British Industry, Britain's leading business lobby.
It said some tightening of the economy was necessary, but given the disappointing recovery in the public finances a fiscal tightening was preferable.
Both major political parties have ruled out unpopular income tax rises after the May 1 election.
Richardson criticised their election promises. "The last thing any government should ever do if it is trying to manage the economy effectively, is to box itself in in this way."
Financial markets expect the next government, of whichever party, to raise the cost of borrowing from 6.0 percent by a quarter or half percentage point.
Richardson said an interest rate rise would only serve to fuel the pound's spirited rally. It is up around 16 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August.

Asked at a news conference if a rate rise would make the pound go higher and stay there, BCC president David Richardson said: "Yes -- you saw what happened after the last rate rise. Fiscal tightening would be much less damaging to the economy than a rate rise."
The BCC said it was very concerned about the decline in exports and the survey showed that in the first quarter exporting activity was at its lowest point for four years.
Its survey showed two thirds of all manufacturers are now seriously concerned about the value of the pound, one third higher than a year ago.
Earlier on Thursday, official figures showed Britain's trade deficit with the rest of the world widened in February as exports dropped off in the face of the strong pound.

The BCC said the survey showed several bright spots in the first quarter including high levels of job creation and investment in both the service and manufacturing sectors, with a notable reduction in capacity utilisation.
"The main black spot is the continuing high levels of recruitment difficulties firms face," the survey said.

Richardson said there was a danger that the high levels of recruitment difficulties could fuel wage inflation. "Since last year, worries by employers of the effect that wage settlements could have on their company have increased considerably."
